(Continuation....starting all the way back on post # 1195)

"How does this special zone manifest itself physically on a chart"

It isn't always so clear. Sometimes I see what I label as a DP without knowing specifically why that zone is the DP. I just "see" the zone and it looks like the place where price made the choice to move up or down. Sometimes this works, but other times it doesn't. I don't like 'winging it' based on what 'looks right'. I know there has to be a specific methodology for defining how to ID the exact DP/FOF.

There must be a logical procedural way of finding the 'heart' of the newly created transaction of FOF.

I am not a doctor... but I know a heart surgeon has to open the rib cage to gain access the heart for a transplant...but if I tried to perform an operation like that I'd just be winging it. Surely the patient would die. A true heart surgeon knows exactly where to open the chest, how to open the rib cage, and how to properly access the heart for transplanting. They don't just do what 'looks' right..they train for years to do it exactly right. I am sure they have a clear methodology for this delicate procedure.

Trading is financial heart surgery. We have to approach it with the same professionalism and dedication to being precise and logical.

Can't we work together to form a type of methodology for finding and properly drawing these origins/DP's? With all of the great info on RTM it seems there is very little information on this topic.

(Continuation....starting all the way back on post # 1195)

Let's start with an example EUR-AUD. The chart below shows three FL Boxes that form an important swap zone.

(I chose this example for a reason...FL Box 3 ends up not holding price and I want to investigate why this happens)

If we were trading this chart live we would be focusing on Box 3. This box represents the place where FOF was created after an engulf of an important swap zone.

As you can see, price comes back to this areas and completely ignores FL Box 3.

Clearly, even if I had found the DP and origin located inside FL Box 3, I would have been stopped out almost immediately.

Why did this happen?

Isn't there an origin located in Box 3 with FOF? There is an important DP in FL Box 3 that acted as the source of a very large move up...so why did price blow through this FL Box? What specific mistake did I make in my analysis that led to this (would-be) failed trade?

1. The FL Boxes look accurate. Each box was formed and held price down. 2. Price was held down and it made a new low/new high as a result in each of the three boxes 3. Price went from buyer control to seller control to buyer control.... swapped completely and FOF was formed as a result 4. There is a clear origin/DP located in FL Box 3

So...what happened? What specific step do I need to add in my analysis to 'filter' out situations like this? This example is not a rarity...these fail ALL THE TIME

There must be more to the analysis.

First, we have to realize the following:

1. Not every origin and DP is going to bounce price. 2. Not every swap zone will lead to a FL Box that contains the DP/Origin to bounce price (even if the FL Boxes are drawn correctly like mine

If these two factors are true, we have to look beyond the FL Boxes and the swap zone to understand the context of what is happening around this area.

Maybe the answer lies in the context of price in and around this area

Let's look at the context:

Hourly chart...zoomed out for reference. I circled the area where price missed FL Box 3.

As you can see from the hourly chart, FL Box 3 was actually pretty close to the area where price ended up bouncing....it missed by a nasty FO. Unfortunately when it comes to trading, 'pretty close' is worthless. I need to be exact.

Here is what I see on the hourly chart:I will circle and number all of the lows that may be relevant to this trade.

I suspect someone is likely to tell me that the FO which occurred at # 7 happened as a reaction to the low made at # 6. To that person, I would ask the following questions:

1. Specifically what DP was price reacting to in low # 6 and how could we have known price was going to FO to that level? What makes the OF in that area so important?

2. If price FO (at #7) because it was reacting off of Low # 6, what kept price from FO even further to react off of Low #4

Under what specific context will price FO to a neighboring high/low? Why does this happen, and when do we know we have reached a place where price will not fake out any lower? As you can see from this chart (and virtually every other chart) there is always a lower low or higher high that price could FO to. We have to place our stop loss somewhere.... There must be an answer to this or associate and master traders would be unable to take the trades they do with such low draw down.

It is usually at this point that someone mentions the issue of true supply/demand & the issue of scale. This is something I have studied a lot yet I struggle to devise a clear methodology for applying it to finding the right location for taking these types of TT.

It is obvious (from all my failed trades) that we can't just trade any swap zone...even if the swap zone is formed nicely with perfectly drawn FL Boxes. The swap zone must occur in a specific location within the scope of all the PA surrounding it. It is this "elusive" location that I have yet to find. Nobody seems to directly disclose what they look for in a location to start drawing swap zones. When the question is asked, the answers are generally equivocal.

This may be because answering the question of 'context' and location of swap zones exposes a great deal of the strategy behind successfully executing these types of trades. If this is true, it is good new because it means we are asking the right questions....

I may be wrong, but I think we can narrow the reasons for the failed trade at Box # 3 as a fakeout forming at circle # 7, as a reaction off something is the low represented by circle # 6.

Fakeouts occur in areas of liquidity - usually to true supply/demand. A FO always has a specific purpose. Anytime we draw swap zones and identify the DP/origin where we expect price to react, we must be sure there are no remaining pockets of FOF remaining below our entry (or above our entry if we are attempting a short trade). I have heard Salivan mention this many times in his posts.

How do we go about making sure there are no pockets of FOF below or above our targeted entry? Isn't there always an area of liquidity below or above our entry if we look hard enough? The answer is yes, of course. Depending on the scale, there might be a hundred areas with FOF located somewhere above or below the targeted entry....knowing that alone doesn't help us at all. The real question is one that involves refining our definition of "areas where pockets of FOF remain". This is technically a true statement, but it is much too general and pretty unhelpful if we don't understand more context and detail.

A more clever question would be:"under what specific circumstances is a pocket of FOF located above/below our targeted entry relevant with regard to a potential FO?

Fakeouts aren't random - they are calculated moves to obtain liquidity. They occur all the time, but I don't think they are as random as they might seem (although I must admit they seem very random at times... )

Then there is the issue of reactive vs. original price action. Often times when we look at a chart like the USD-CHF example used in this posting, we see multiple lows and think they are all independently formed, when in reality they are often just a reaction off a different zone...it might be a reaction from a HTF area of true supply/demand but it also might just be a reaction of another reaction that is a reaction off a HTF area of true supply/demand.

To complicate this further, even in a situation where price is just reacting off a different level, the reaction itself is forming an independent true supply/demand level on a LTF chart. It is just in a different scale. So essentially, what we have is a whole bunch of reactions off other reactions that create new reactions. All these newly created reactions include smaller areas of true supply/demand (original supply/demand that is formed independent of any reaction) and within their smaller scales price will react to these levels accordingly. All of these originally formed areas of true supply/demand have their own MPL's which dictate how far price is likely to FO. How do we know which scales are relevant and which ones are not relevant when it comes to our trade setups? Again, I repeat the question I asked above: "under what specific circumstances is a pocket of FOF located above/below our targeted entry relevant with regard to a potential FO?

I think the answer to many of our failed trades can be found in answering these questions. We need to know which pockets of FOF (another way of saying this is "we need to know which areas of true supply/demand") are relevant to a possible FO occurring at our entry point.

(Continuation....starting all the way back on post # 1195)

An important question to ask prior to drawing the FL Boxes and looking for a trade: "is the area where I am drawing my FL Boxes (and identifying the swap zone that will lead to my entry) a reaction to a different zone"?

Example: I circled the swap 'area of interest' in neon green in the chart below. what is this whole area a reaction to?

It seems that all the PA in the neon green circle, and the subsequent low @ # 6, is all just a reaction off of low #4 to the left.

In summary:

1. The FO which ruined my original trade setup happened at point # 7

2. The FO at point 7 was a reaction to the low formed at point # 6

3. The low at point # 6 is a reaction to the low previously formed at # 4

All of these 'reactions' are dependent on whatever they are reacting to on the left, but they are also forming a DBR which will form an original (non reactive) true supply/demand zone that has an MPL.

(Continuation)

Is the following statement true?

** The FO that ruined my trade setup @ # 7 is reacting off of a pocket of FOF existing at low # 6. This pocket of FOF located at low #6 is an area of true demand originally formed from the DBR that formed as a result of low # 6 reacting to low #4.

(chart copied over from previous post for reference)

If my question above is indeed correct, and #7 is reacting off of FOF located in low #6, could this failed trade have been avoided by anticipating FO # 7?

If yes, my next question: Assuming there was no FOF left in the low at #6, could price still FO @ low # 7 but drop further to get available orders at low # 4 (assuming there was available FOF at low #4). In other words, is a potential FO limited to hitting the nearest reaction level or can it FO as far as it wants until it finds FOF? What limits how far price can FO in search of FOF?

Here is a quick reminder of the initial trade example that started this whole analysis (for those who started reading half way through the other posts)

The basic premise for all this posting is finding out why price didn't react at FL Box 3, and finding ways to avoid a failed trade like this in the future.

The pair is EUR-AUD

** If we are saying # 7 is a FO to get FOF that is originally formed at # 6 (true demand), then how do we find the true demand of # 6 to determine if there is actually FOF available? If I am going to avoid a bad trade in the future, I need to look left and see what possible FOF exists to attract a FO (like a magnet, price is attracted to areas of FOF).

I also want to reiterate: even though we know # 6 is just a reaction to # 4 (further to the left) we know all DBR reactions do create an area of original true supply/demand (FOF) on a smaller scale. It is this originally formed FOF (smaller scale) that we are looking for as an indication that price might FO.

To find true demand & FOF in DBR # 6 I have to refer back to my post about 4 hours ago... refer back to post #1200

Hi H, I see from your latest posts that you put in a lot of work and determination to understand the market and RTM. I also sense a bit of frustration which I totally understand. IMHO you are fine with market structure ie. identifying FL (true S/D) and FO vs eng.

The next part which helps to stick it all together is the psychology of ITs. In my opinion, we can't know which level is likely to hold unless we consider this, because ITs or smart money decides which level they want to sell/buy at. Remember we look for tricks into a zone where a trick was played. If there are no tricks on approach including manipulation of hope and fear then there's simply no trade because there are no signs a level is going to hold. Sometimes a level is fine to TT because of past tricks played at a zone which in itself is a very good place, for example an MPL or FTRFO within a FL aligned with a HTF QM level (FO/trick level), but then unless PA kicks in to let us hold that trade we must get out at first trouble area or cover enough for a possible stop as there are no clues for further IT intentions.

I'm no master at this, I lose too, but understanding this helps to filter out a lot of losing trades. Check the dissection thread, all setups have something in common, the manipulation of retailers (approach and/or history).

For example recent GU trade you took. It was a solid FL with CP on approach, could work and wasn't really a bad trade. The thing is the context of what happened before it. Price approached an origin and then engulfed up, after the eng up, price FO into the lowest possible QM in that zone and respected it with buying signs. Knowing this means a trick was played into a past trick zone (QM), so the intention of ITs are likely long than short although we have still a previous eng to the downside in play and price might still follow this but we also know the market doesn't move in straight lines and a RT is always possible. BTW when an origin is respected and an eng happens this is a big warning sign for a possible RT, independently of HTF engulf cycles.

Another aha moment I had recently was to not follow strictly the rules about higher/lower scale FL boxes and engulfs but instead trying to see the orders (true S/D) and the context in which they happen.

Wish you good luck and I hope someone more experienced can help you with some important questions you asked above

Would it be accurate to say every FTB to a FL is essentially a FO on a LTF scale?

The FO takes the form of a RBD reaction to the True supply level on the left, and whether the new true supply level (true supply 2) formed by the RBD is tradeable depends on whether the FO reached the extreme set of orders (MPL) in the FL it is a reaction to. If not, a FO could still occur to MPL 1 for the remaining FOF.

That would explain why only some QM setups work... every QM has a FO (the LL or HH). Whether the QM is tradeable depends on whether or not the FO reached the extreme set of orders in the FL it is reacting to (to the left). If yes, there is no need to worry about another FO...the FOF is gone from this level. The next area of FOF would occur in the FL that forms after the EG of the DP to FO...the new 'true supply' level where FOF has been created.

It just so happens this new FOF often occurs at a the 'QM' level (more or less equal to the left shoulder of the QM) because the high of the left shoulder of a QM is where a decision is made to FO...the engulf of that important DP would occur very near to the top of that shoulder...
